tip: A Korean question is just a statement with rising tone – no 'do', no word flip: 먹어요 (meogeoyo) covers both 'I eat' and 'are you eating?'.
English drags 'where' to the front; Korean leaves it next to the verb: 화장실이 어디예요? (hwajangsil-i eodi-yeyo?) is literally 'the bathroom is where?'.
Korean rarely says 'he' or 'she' – you say 그 사람 (geu saram = that person) instead, even where English would use a pronoun.
No 'for' after waiting: 기다려요 (gidaryeoyo = wait) takes a direct object, so it's 누구를 (nugu-reul = whom), not 'for whom'.
랑 (rang) is the casual spoken 'with', glued to the end of its noun: 누구랑 (nugu-rang = with whom). Formal or written Korean uses 와/과 (wa/gwa) instead.
No 'your' needed – Korean drops possessives when context is clear: 생일이 언제예요? (saengil-i eonje-yeyo?) is just 'when is birthday?', understood as yours.
Negation is the tiny word 안 (an) placed right before the verb: 안 먹어요 (an meogeoyo = not eating). No 'don't' verb needed.
'How do I get there?' has no 'get' or 'there' in Korean – 가다 (gada = go) does the work: 어떻게 가요? (eotteoke gayo?) is just 'how go?'.
The count comes after the thing counted: 사과 한 개 (sagwa han gae = apple, one item) – noun first, then number and counter, the reverse of 'one apple'.
'Have' is really 'exist': 동생이 두 명 있어요 (dongsaeng-i du myeong isseoyo) = 'two younger siblings exist'. Korean states existence, not ownership.
'Not have' is its own verb 없어요 (eopseoyo), never 안 있어요 (an isseoyo): 돈이 없어요 (don-i eopseoyo = there is no money).
시 (si) = o'clock, 시간 (sigan) = hours of duration: 한 시간 걸려요 (han sigan geollyeoyo) = 'it takes one hour', not one o'clock.
일 (il) means work, day, and the number one – context decides. In 일이 어때요? (ir-i eottaeyo? = how is work?) it's your job.
